iterations.theme: Modern dating, male-female relationships, and the challenges of approaching

sections.subtitle: Modern dating under the magnifying glass: Who approaches whom today and why?
sections.screenshot_description: Host Marko introduces the viewers and interlocutors to the topic of modern dating and approaching.
sections.content:
In the new episode of the show **Generacija plus** on Laudato TV, host Marko opens a topic that, due to current social circumstances and the challenges young people face, has become unavoidable – **modern dating** and the issue of approaching. How to establish first contact, how to recognize if a relationship is going in a good direction, and whether making the first move is still exclusively a man's job or if the burden has fallen on the backs of girls, are just some of the questions that found their way onto the table.

So that the discussion would not go in too broad a direction, Marko, together with his interlocutors – Luka, Andrija, and two female guests – structures the conversation through five key phases of male-female getting to know each other:

- **Signs of interest** and recognizing mutual attraction
- **Approaching** and taking the initiative
- **Red flags** in behavior
- **Unrealistic expectations** versus healthy standards
- **The look of the first date** and the dynamics of dating itself

sections.subtitle: Signs of interest, female guard, and the unavoidable importance of physical attraction
sections.screenshot_description: The female guest explains how true signs of interest are best recognized only when casual communication begins.
sections.content:
The discussion begins with the eternal dilemma: how to know that someone likes us and when to take the first step? One of the female guests right at the beginning expresses regret that many young men today wait for explicit signs (so-called *hints*) before they even try to approach a girl. She points out that from her perspective, if she were in the place of a man who likes a girl, she would not be able to sleep peacefully without at least trying something, even without a return signal.

Luka agrees that it is more natural when contact happens spontaneously through joint gatherings or glances, but he believes that a man, if he likes a girl for a longer time, should definitely approach regardless of return steps. Andrija, on the other hand, notes that he personally would not approach a girl "out of nowhere" exclusively on the basis of physical attraction at first sight, rather it is important to him to previously get to know her character at least a little and see if there is a basic openness for communication in her.

When it comes to recognizing concrete signs in shared circles or prayer communities, the interlocutor explains that frequent glances during the evening are by no means imagined, rather courage is often lacking on both sides. However, true interest is best revealed only when a young man starts casual communication. Then body language reveals everything:

- **Signs of interest:** a smile, active participation in the conversation, and asking follow-up questions.
- **Signs of disinterest:** communication exclusively out of politeness (so that the girl does not rudely reject the young man), answering with "yes" or "no", turning the body to the other side, and avoiding eye contact.

Marko follows up with an observation from male circles, pointing out how girls in prayer communities often keep too high a guard and do not allow themselves to be won over because "they are all waiting for Saint Joseph", and when someone like that appears, then he is not interesting enough for them. In doing so, he very directly emphasizes how **physical attraction is the foundation of every approach**. Although in religious circles falling in love with the soul and eternity is often emphasized, Marko considers it illusory to start anything with a person who is not physically attractive to us: *"She cannot be Mother Teresa, if she is not physically beautiful to me, it's in vain. I cannot be with someone who is not physically attractive to me."*

sections.subtitle: The first step as a man's task: "A woman who approaches a man, approaches out of desperation"
sections.screenshot_description: Andrija explains why he finds it repulsive when a girl takes the initiative first and approaches a man.
sections.content:
To the question of whether girls or men themselves are to blame for today's passivity of young men, the female guest believes that an unnecessary fuss has been created around the fear of rejection. Unless a girl is extremely rude and mocks the young man in front of others – in which case the young man can be grateful to God that he avoided such a person – rejection is not the worst thing in the world. Moreover, she izuzetno respects every young man who gathers the courage and approaches, even if she rejects him, while she considers those who despite obvious liking never do anything to be cowards. She concludes that the core of the problem is in the fact that **today's girls lack femininity, and young men lack masculinity**.

All the male participants in the studio agree on one thing: direct approaching and asking for a date are exclusively a man's job. Andrija reveals how situations in which girls approached him first were a big *turn-off* for him because that does not correspond to the male and female character. His stance is that a woman can subtly create an opportunity or an environment in which she is available, but the man is the one who must make a concrete step. He also encourages young people who go to Christian camps and community meetings that, although it does not have to be their primary goal, they should at least be open to meeting people of similar beliefs.

Marko, in his recognizable, direct tone, says that he would "ban by law" taken people from going to summer camps, and about female approaching he states a very firm stance: *"To me personally, a woman who approaches a man, approaches out of desperation. There is so much nothing anywhere anymore, or everything is so sluggish, that she has to take herself out and be the man in that relationship. I simply cannot take seriously a girl who approaches me."*

The female guest confirms that she herself would never do that either because the whole time she would have the feeling that the entire relationship is based on her initiative, although she admits that some male friends tell her that it would be easier for them if girls approached them. Luka, who is married and thereby, as the interlocutors jokingly say, the most qualified to give advice, agrees that a direct female pass is repulsive, except perhaps in situations when two people already move in the same circle of friends and the young man already likes that girl from earlier. The second female guest and Luka also warn of frequent misunderstandings: from young men who behave too friendly and thus leave the wrong impression, to female friends who artificially "pump up" the story about liking where there actually isn't any.

sections.subtitle: Virtual courage, lack of social skills, and fear of exclusivity
sections.screenshot_description: Andrija and Luka talk about the false security behind the screen and the loss of social skills in the digital age.
sections.content:
Why is it easier for today's young men to send a message on Instagram, TikTok, or Snapchat than to approach a girl in person? Andrija sees the problem in **false courage behind the screen** and the unwillingness of young people to step out of their own comfort zone. Typing a message enables calculating and avoiding discomfort, while the courage for a face-to-face encounter is lost. Besides that, Andrija points out how the widespread consumption of pornography deeply disrupts a man's view of a woman and creates a blockage in real approaching.

Luka and the second female guest follow up with the problem of the **lack of social skills** in the digital age. Due to the lack of practice in real contact, it has become extremely difficult for young people to act spontaneously, so every ordinary step looks like a "big project" to them that requires long-term planning. The first female guest still defends social networks in situations when two people do not have the opportunity to see each other in person, noting that many successful couples started their relationship precisely with an online message. However, Marko draws a clear line between reaching out to a person we already know and randomly reaching out to unknown girls based on a profile, which he considers completely meaningless. Quoting his ex-girlfriend, he concludes: *"Who wants to, finds a way, who doesn't want to, finds an excuse."*

Referring to the claim of a female psychologist, Marko points out how men today do not develop social skills even among themselves – for example, at football sessions they barely greet each other and do not connect in life at all, so it is no wonder that they do not know how to approach women either. Along with the fear of rejection, Marko lists three more key brakes in today's men:

1. **Shame:** Young men have become sluggish and are afraid to overcome their own shame of possible failure.
2. **Unwillingness for sacrifice and change:** The awareness that a successful approach could lead to a relationship, and a real relationship requires renunciation, sacrifice, and working on oneself, for which many are not ready.
3. **Fear of exclusivity:** Under the influence of social networks and pornography, it is difficult for men to maintain an exclusive view toward only one woman.

Marko emphasizes how the fundamental rule of dating is precisely **exclusivity** – a conscious decision that, despite the fact that in the world there are probably prettier, smarter, or more pious girls, you choose precisely that one person in order to see where your relationship can go. Such determination, he concludes, God always blesses, either by entering into a relationship, or by a clear realization that you are not for each other.

sections.subtitle: Red flags: From passivity and rudeness to family background
sections.screenshot_description: The female interlocutors explain what they consider the biggest 'red flags' in men when getting to know each other.
sections.content:
In the part of the conversation dedicated to the so-called red flags (*red flags*), the girls very clearly defined what immediately repels them in men. For the first female guest, the biggest minus is the **lack of initiative and life ambition**. If a young man invites a girl on a date, and has not planned where they will go at all, or if in general in life he has no desire to work, earn, and one day provide for a family, rather depends on his parents' allowance, such passivity is completely unmasculine for her.

The second female guest focuses on behavior and self-care, singling out two main points:
- **Attitude toward workers in service industries:** If a young man is unkind or impolite toward waiters, salespeople, or delivery workers, this shows that he is kind only toward those from whom he has some benefit.
- **Extremes in self-care:** Excessive care about appearance leaves an impression of self-complacency and egocentrism, while complete neglect toward basic hygiene and oneself raises the question of how he will one day be able to care for a wife and family.

From the male side, Andrija highlights as a key criterion the **girl's relationship with her family**. Since a healthy family forms healthy persons, the way a girl communicates with her parents and close ones is a strong indicator for him of her spiritual background and maturity. Luka, on the other hand, lists as problematic girls who have a stubborn guard and are not humble and open enough for solving problems through conversation. Also, willingness to sacrifice for a future marriage and family is extremely important to him, noticing how many of today's girls are lost in the transition between traditional upbringing and modern influences.

Marko prepared an entire list of things to which he pays attention. The first is the **presence of a healthy father figure** in the girl's life (whether through a father, uncle, professor, or priest). He explains how a girl who does not know what a man should be like often projects unrealistic images onto her partner, forcing him to step out of his own identity. Furthermore, Marko singles out:

- **Excessive makeup:** Personally, an unnatural look strongly repels him, vividly commenting how at about twenty weddings in the last two years he has almost not seen naturally made-up girls (*"so much makeup that her Face ID on her mobile phone doesn't work"*).
- **Communication of past wounds:** He is aware that women psychologically bear traumas from previous relationships much harder and open up again with more difficulty, but he considers it beautiful when a girl knows how to honestly communicate that and gradually build trust.
- **Own life and female friends:** Marko points out that he could not be with a girl who does not have female friends, hobbies, and her own obligations and is available to him at literally every moment. Such dependence makes an idol out of a partner, and he does not want to be in the place of God in her life.

sections.subtitle: Standards versus ideals: What makes true femininity and masculinity today?
sections.screenshot_description: The second female guest talks about how true femininity manifests primarily through the capacity to love and openness toward others.
sections.content:
Speaking about the criteria when choosing a partner, the interlocutors agree that expectations today are often unrealistically high. The female guest notes how young men under the influence of the internet create a distorted picture of female appearance, while girls often put together endless lists of traits that an ideal man would have to have, instead of observing the real person standing in front of them. An additional problem is the **hyperinflation of choice** – from dating applications to large gatherings of young people at places like Zagreb's Jarun, where in a sea of beautiful girls young men cannot make a decision for just one because they are constantly looking for perfection. In doing so, Marko introduces an important distinction between **ideals** (what we strive for) and **standards** (the minimum below which one does not go).

To the question of what makes a woman feminine, the second female guest answers that it is primarily **knowing how to love** – openness to others, readiness to help, listening, and virtues that stem from a relationship with the Lord. The first female guest adds that tenderness and readiness to leave the leadership to the man (without constant complaining for every little thing) are key, with the note that every girl expresses femininity in her own, authentic way, preparing herself thus for submission in love as is lived in marriage.

When it comes to **masculinity**, the male part of the studio presents clear guidelines:

- **Andrija:** A man must be direct and clearly communicate his intentions in a relationship, be decisive (keep his word), prudent, and above all through prayer submit his desires to God's will.
- **Luka:** For Catholics, the fundamental standard is openness to faith, a shared life in God, and openness to life in marriage. A man must from the very beginning set a clear direction, be active, disciplined, and with his life be an example to his future wife and children.
- **Marko:** Referring to **Saint Thomas Aquinas**, who defines effeminacy as the refusal to bear things that are arduous and difficult, Marko criticizes modern trends among men (waxing, wearing makeup, overly tight and overly short pants) and claims that a man who does not know how to change a lightbulb, mow the grass, or assemble a desk has no business in marriage. He also mentions **Aristotle's** concept of order (God, then others, then me), warning that people today often build their value on what they possess (car, apartment, and even a partner as a trophy), instead of on what they themselves can offer.

Special emphasis was placed on male **consistency and integrity**. Marko and the female guests, through humorous examples (such as ignoring lit warning lights in a car or a broken air conditioner) and Luka's joke about a man who knocked down a house with a car and only said *"sorry"* instead of fixing the damage, conclude: if a man is not active, diligent, and consistent in small, everyday promises, he will not be a pillar in big life matters either.

sections.subtitle: First date without pressure, frequency of seeing each other, and final encouragement for singles
sections.screenshot_description: The interlocutors discuss what the first date should look like and why it should not be taken too dramatically.
sections.content:
In the final part of the show, the conversation moves to the concrete realization of the first date. The first female guest points out how young people must relax and realize that **the first coffee is not a promise of marriage nor entering into a relationship**. A girl who agrees to a date has not thereby promised anything, just as a young man does not thereby sign a contract, therefore there is no need to create too much pressure.

Marko, on the other hand, provokes a discussion with the claim that on the first date one should not go for coffee at all. Sitting in a cafe for two to three hours across from a person we barely know he considers an unnatural environment that often turns into a dry filling out of a "lexicon" (questions about school, work, and family). Instead of that, he suggests a more active date like a walk. However, Luka and the female guests do not agree completely – Luka believes that a walk is much more intimate and is better for a second or third date, while coffee is a necessary first step that simply needs to be passed, even if it is a bit awkward in the beginning.

As for the frequency of seeing each other, Luka explains that it depends on the life phase of the couple. For mature persons who work and are ready to quickly enter into marriage, it might be enough to see each other once to twice a week, while for him and his wife in the beginning it was necessary to see each other three to four times a week in order for things to get moving. Andrija adds how it is key to recognize the **love languages** of the other person – for someone, precisely shared time is the main proof of affection, while for others gifts or words of praise are more important, but in everything one should maintain a healthy measure.

For the very end, the participants send a strong encouragement to all those who have been single for a long time and believe in the lie that they will never find anyone:

- **Creating opportunities (Andrija):** Girls need to step out of closedness in social situations. As an example, he cites weddings at which single girls often dance with one another, instead of sitting at a table and thereby giving a clear sign to young men that they are single and open for an invitation to dance.
- **Stepping out of the comfort zone (First female guest):** A partner will not fall from the sky; for good things in life it is necessary to grit one's teeth and make an effort, even when approaching or opening up is not easy.
- **Courage and creativity (Luka):** If it is difficult for a young man to immediately invite a girl one-on-one, he can always be creative and organize a joint gathering through friends in order to break the ice more easily.
- **Change of environment (Second female guest):** If a girl sees that in her current circle there is no one interesting, she must not remain passive in the same place, rather she needs to go out into new environments.

Marko concludes the show in a humorous tone, advising young men to freely "play the piety card" on a date and ask the girl if Saint Joseph is her favorite saint too, which certainly buys them four hours of conversation, with a final message to everyone that dating is a wonderful thing for which it is worth daring.
keywords: stepping out of the comfort zone
